draft.title: The Light Horse in the Middle East
card: The Australian Light Horse were mounted troops. They rode horses to move fast across open country, then dismounted and fought on foot with rifles.
From 1916 they fought the Ottoman Empire, an ally of Germany, in the deserts of Sinai and then in Palestine. This was a different kind of war from the trenches of the Western Front.
Water was a major problem. Armies needed wells to supply men and horses, so capturing wells could decide a battle.
At Beersheba on 31 October 1917, Light Horse troops charged on horseback at the Ottoman trenches. They reached the town and captured its wells, which helped open the way into Palestine.
draft.remember: The Light Horse used speed and horses in the desert, and the Beersheba charge won wells that opened Palestine.

a.q: Why did the Light Horse want to capture Beersheba in 1917?
opts: Its wells gave water for men and horses
Its harbour let ships reach Gallipoli
Its trenches linked up with the Western Front
Its railway led straight to Germany
a.why: Beersheba had wells, and water was vital in the desert for men and horses. The harbour option is tempting because of Gallipoli, but Beersheba was an inland town in Palestine and Gallipoli was a separate campaign.
a.clue: Think about what soldiers and horses need in a desert.

b.q: Which describes how the Light Horse usually fought in Sinai and Palestine?
opts: They rode to the fight, then often fought on foot
They stayed in long trench lines for years
They landed from ships onto steep cliffs
They fought only from the saddle with swords
b.why: Light Horse troops used horses for speed, then usually dismounted and fought with rifles. The Beersheba charge was unusual, so the idea that they only fought from the saddle is wrong.
b.clue: The horses were mainly for movement across open country.

a.best: Its wells gave water for men and horses

b.best: They rode to the fight, then often fought on foot

problems.detail: The remember line says the Beersheba wells 'opened Palestine', but the card more carefully says capturing them 'helped open the way into Palestine'. The remember line overstates what the card teaches.

check.summary: Facts and answers check out: the Light Horse were mounted infantry, they fought in Sinai from 1916, and Beersheba was charged on 31 October 1917 to capture its wells. One small issue: the remember line overstates the card by saying the wells 'opened Palestine' rather than 'helped open the way'.
